summary:
Bryansk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies across all of the country's regions. The UK Home Office country policy note on Russia (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) records no region-specific findings: it sets the national conditions in force here as everywhere else in Russia.

Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention; repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist makes participation punishable by two to six years' imprisonment and organising by six to ten years.

Between December 2022 and March 2024, at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. The Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates, and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters.

Between January 2024 and June 2025, at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. A further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison.

On 15 May 2025, investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, facing up to 12 years in prison.

A foreign government's travel advisory for Russia states that its official support for nationals is 'very limited' in parts of the country.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement climate documented by Human Rights Watch is national in scope, with no region-specific findings isolating Bryansk Oblast from the pattern of extremism designations, administrative symbol-display cases, and criminal prosecutions recorded elsewhere in Russia.

The Home Office note's assessment that trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates face likely persecution sets the standard for UK asylum claims and reflects conditions that apply uniformly across Russian regions, including Bryansk Oblast.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bryansk Oblast face the same legal exposure as elsewhere in Russia: no discrimination legislation covers housing, healthcare or employment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender recognition and trans-specific healthcare are unavailable.

Local courts handle anti-LGBT+ enforcement under the same statutes, with administrative fines for symbol display and criminal exposure for repeat propaganda or extremism-related offences.
outOfScopeNotes:
No region-specific enforcement data for Bryansk Oblast is sourced; the figures cited (101 convictions, 139 people affected, 20 criminal charges) are national totals and their distribution across oblasts is not resolved in the inventory.

The inventory does not source any Bryansk Oblast-specific incidents of violence, raids, or detentions against trans people; whether local enforcement diverges from the national pattern is not established.
